clue.text: Comatose on the settee, perhaps, taking in 'Howard's end'

indicators.note: taking in means the seating word swallows another letter inside it

parts.note: someone on a settee is sitting down, i.e. seated; 'perhaps' marks the settee as just one example of a seat

indicators.note: end picks out the final letter of the name Howard

explanation.surface: Someone dozing on the sofa while a television adaptation of Howards End plays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking in' puts D, the last letter of Howard (the possessive 's adds nothing), inside SEATED. The quotation marks dress it up as the Forster novel title.
explanation.definitionFit: A drugged or heavily calmed person may be insensible, which is what comatose loosely describes.

clue.text: Perceives a wife as a plaything

parts.note: to perceive is to see, so 'perceives' gives sees
W is the standard abbreviation for wife, as in genealogy tables

explanation.surface: A husband regards his spouse as a mere toy.
explanation.definitionFit: A playground toy on which two children tip up and down is a classic plaything.

indicators.note: enters means the club word goes inside the river word

parts.note: a banker in crosswords is a river (it has banks); the Dee is a British river
a bat is a club used in sports such as cricket and baseball

explanation.surface: A sports club holds talks with its bank manager.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banker' looks like a financier, but in crosswords it is something with banks, a river: here the DEE, which flows through Wales and England.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal argument between opposing sides is a structured discussion.

clue.text: They hailed from various corners with no end of rubbish!

indicators.note: various suggests the letters of corners come in varied order
rubbish as a verb means to mess up, so this marks the letters as jumbled
no end tells us to cut the last letter off the word with

explanation.surface: People shouting their rubbish from street corners all over town.
explanation.walkthrough: Two anagram signals share the work: 'various' and 'of rubbish' (rubbish as a verb, to mess up). Before newspapers, a bellman called out public notices in the street.
explanation.definitionFit: Official criers in old towns called out, or hailed, the public with news and proclamations.

indicators.note: embraces means the female word wraps around the about word

parts.note: a dam is a female parent, especially of a horse or other animal
re is Latin-derived for about or concerning, as in business letters

explanation.surface: Someone's romantic daydream about a woman hugging them.
explanation.definitionFit: A dream can be a waking fancy, a wish or imagined scenario, the same thing as a fantasy.

indicators.note: following places the levelled word after the Roman number

parts.note: in Roman numerals C is 100 and L is 50, so 150 is CL
to level a gun is to point it, so levelled means aimed

explanation.surface: A score of 150 was levelled and the innings declared, cricket-style.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a side 'declares' to close its innings; here declared simply means stated. Levelled means pointed, as a weapon is.
explanation.definitionFit: To claim something is to assert or state it openly, so claimed is a synonym of declared.

parts.note: C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
a lien is a legal right to hold another's property until a debt is paid
tele is a short informal word for television

explanation.surface: Gamblers are caught on camera on television.
explanation.walkthrough: Punters is British slang for customers (as well as gamblers), which makes it fit a body of customers. 'on' works as a link joining the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Punters is British slang for paying customers, and the collective body of customers is a business's clientele.

clue.text: A veto from chirac following shortly

parts.note: Jacques Chirac was French president, and a French veto is non, French for no

explanation.surface: A French president's refusal comes soon after.
explanation.walkthrough: 'following' is a link: the definition 'shortly' follows the wordplay. NON is French for no, as a French president might say in vetoing something.
explanation.definitionFit: Anon is an old-fashioned word meaning soon, in a little while.

indicators.note: under, in a down clue, puts the tarry word below the sea word

parts.note: the main is a poetic word for the open sea, as in the Spanish Main
to tarry is to linger or stay

explanation.surface: A tar-covered anchor lying on the seabed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'undersea' reads as one word but splits as 'under', placing one piece below in this down clue, and 'sea'. Tarry looks like 'covered in tar' but is the verb meaning linger.
explanation.definitionFit: An anchor in the figurative sense is the chief support of something, its principal prop.

clue.text: More than one man allied to Leeds united?

definitions.text: More than one man allied to Leeds united?

indicators.note: united here signals joining the two words and merging them into a new order

explanation.surface: Several fans loyal to Leeds United football club.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: men of the Yorkshire Dales live near Leeds, a city in Yorkshire. Leeds United is a football club, so 'united' looks like part of its name.
explanation.definitionFit: Natives of the Yorkshire Dales are inhabitants of the area around Leeds, so plural Yorkshiremen tied to that region.

parts.note: reads like a remote pub or nightclub, but means a body joint used to push people out of the way

explanation.surface: A remote, hard-to-find bar or nightclub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' suggests a dive or bar; it is the arm joint, and to use it is to shove someone aside.
explanation.definitionFit: The arm's middle joint is used to nudge people aside, hence the verb meaning to push out of the way.

parts.note: looks like a telegraph wire, but means the stated opinion of the Daily Telegraph newspaper

explanation.surface: A telegraph wire strung between poles.
explanation.walkthrough: The Daily Telegraph, which published this puzzle, sets out its official position or 'line' in a leading article.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper's leading article gives the paper's official stance, its party line on an issue.

definitions.meaning: a bond is a tie or emotional connection between people
an accessory is an extra part fitted to a device, such as a vacuum cleaner nozzle

explanation.surface: James Bond's gadget, as supplied by Q.
explanation.definitionFit: An emotional tie is one sense and an add-on fitting to a tool is the other, both common meanings of the word.

definitions.meaning: the Thames at Oxford is traditionally called by this name
the Egyptian mother goddess, wife of Osiris

explanation.surface: A deity who presides over a river.
explanation.walkthrough: Oxford rowers call the stretch of the Thames through the city by this name.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both the Oxford name for the upper Thames and the chief goddess of ancient Egypt.

parts.note: reads as a messy piece of research, but means the study of mental disorders

explanation.surface: A chaotic, poorly organised piece of research.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disordered' looks like 'untidy'; read it as 'of disorders': the medical field concerned with mental illness.
explanation.definitionFit: The branch of medicine treating mental illnesses is a study of disorders of the mind.

clue.text: It describes movements as earth circles irregularly

indicators.note: irregularly means the letters of the two words are set out in no regular order

explanation.surface: The planet wobbles in an uneven orbit, and something measures its motion.
explanation.walkthrough: The movements are earth tremors: the scale rates the strength of earthquakes. 'as' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: This logarithmic scale grades the magnitude of earthquakes, so it describes ground movements.

parts.note: reads as an answer to a scandal, but a shock is a mass of hair and a solution is a liquid mixture

explanation.surface: A tabloid-style outcry, followed by a proposed fix.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'shock' of hair is a thick unruly mass, and 'solution' means a liquid, not an answer: the lacquer that tames a horrible mop.
explanation.definitionFit: A lacquer sprayed on to hold a wild mop in place is a liquid remedy for unruly locks.

clue.text: Official document's put before Tory leader

indicators.note: put before places the document word ahead of the leading letter

parts.note: a diploma is a certificate document; the 's stands for 'is'

indicators.note: leader picks out the first letter of Tory

explanation.surface: An official paper is handed to the head of the Conservative party.
explanation.definitionFit: An envoy representing a state abroad is a government official.

clue.text: Ghostly appearance has head removed and held in both hands

indicators.note: has head removed means the first letter comes off the appearance word

parts.note: aspect means the look or appearance of something

indicators.note: held in means the removed leading letter is placed between the two hand letters

parts.note: R and L are the abbreviations for right and left, the two hands
aspect means the look or appearance of something

explanation.surface: A ghost carrying its own severed head in both hands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has head removed' takes A off ASPECT to leave SPECT; that same A is then 'held in' R and L (right and left hands), giving RAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Spectral describes something like a spectre or phantom, hence ghostly.

clue.text: Northeast recipe — mash with mint sauce

indicators.note: to mash is to crush and mix, so the letters are pulped into a new order

parts.note: NE is the compass abbreviation for northeast

explanation.surface: A regional recipe for mashed potato served with mint sauce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sauce' is not the condiment but British slang for cheek or insolence.
explanation.definitionFit: Sauce in informal British usage means cheeky rudeness, the same as insolence.

clue.text: Diamonds — initially rock-hard — often make beautiful items

indicators.note: initially means take the opening letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: Diamonds start as very hard rock and are often made into lovely jewellery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rock-hard' counts as two words, giving R and H.
explanation.definitionFit: A diamond shape is a rhombus, a four-sided figure with equal sides; the plural is the Latin form.

clue.text: Having debarked tree sitting on root of iron

indicators.note: sitting on, in a down clue, puts the tree on top of the iron source

parts.note: the ash is a common tree
iron comes from ore, its natural source or root

explanation.surface: A tree with its bark stripped, standing on iron-rich ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'debarked' suggests stripping bark from the tree; it means disembarked, off the ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Passengers who have left a ship are on land, which is what ashore means.

definitions.meaning: short for locomotive, the engine that pulls a train
crazy, from the Spanish word for insane, used in American slang

explanation.surface: Someone obsessed with trains, a railway enthusiast.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a clipped form of locomotive and also slang for crazy.

clue.text: A rocker's keeping his rocky surprises…

indicators.note: keeping means the rocker word holds the scrambled letters inside it

parts.note: a rocker could be a member of the Rolling Stones, and the possessive gives the S

indicators.note: rocky means unsteady, so the letters of his are shaken up

explanation.surface: A rock musician's unsteady performance comes as a surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeping' puts ISH (an anagram of HIS, from 'rocky') inside; the ellipsis ties this clue to the next two in the puzzle and plays no part in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To astonish someone is to amaze or surprise them greatly.

indicators.note: without opening means the first letter of the cooks word is dropped

parts.note: to roast is to cook in an oven, so cooks gives roasts

explanation.surface: Chefs working without opening the ovens.
explanation.walkthrough: An oast is a kiln for drying hops, found in Kent, so a kind of oven.
explanation.definitionFit: These kilns dry hops for brewing, a type of oven.

clue.text: In which the meaning is taken

definitions.text: In which the meaning is taken

indicators.note: In signals that the answer sits inside the run of letters that follows

explanation.surface: A place where a meaning is understood.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across 'meaninG IS Taken', and the whole clue also defines it: the essence of a text is what is taken as its meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The essential sense of a speech or text is its core point, what a listener takes away.

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother
to till soil is to dig it
RA stands for Royal Academician, a British artist; the 's adds the S

explanation.surface: A mother, a farmer and a painter at a celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: RA (Royal Academician) is a member of the Royal Academy of Arts in London. 'Till' is the verb meaning cultivate, not the cash register.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrove Tuesday carnival celebrations, famous in New Orleans, are a festival.

definitions.text: time for a piece of music

parts.words: time for a piece of music
parts.note: describes the speed at which a composition is to be played

explanation.surface: A moment to listen to a tune.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as 'a moment for music', but means the pace at which music is played.
explanation.definitionFit: Musicians use the Italian term for the speed or pace at which a work is played.

clue.text: He wrote play about 'lost at sea'

indicators.note: about means the play word goes around the other letters

parts.note: to toy with something is to play with it

indicators.note: at sea means confused or adrift, so the letters of lost are jumbled

explanation.surface: A writer produced a play about a shipwreck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts OLST (an anagram of LOST, from 'at sea') inside; the quotation marks make 'lost at sea' look like the play's title.
explanation.definitionFit: The Russian author of War and Peace is a famous writer.

parts.note: reads as slang for being crazy, but describes an ascetic living on top of a pillar

explanation.surface: Someone has gone mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up the pole' is British slang for mad; here literally, as early Christian ascetics lived atop pillars.
explanation.definitionFit: Early Christian ascetics such as Simeon lived on top of columns, so they were literally atop a pillar.
